blocks.prompt: Four Bodies, One Bug
blocks.text: A ladybug lays her eggs in a small yellow bunch. She sticks them under a leaf where tiny green bugs are already munching. In a few days the eggs hatch. What crawls out is not a ladybug. It is long and black and spiky, like a tiny dragon. It is called a larva, and it is very hungry. It eats the little green bugs all day long. It grows so fast that its skin splits and it climbs out with a bigger one. Then it glues its tail to a leaf and stops moving. Inside, it is changing. A week later the case cracks open. Out steps a ladybug, soft and pale. Its shell hardens. Its red color and black spots come in. Then it flies.

blocks.prompt: The Beetle With Four Different Bodies
blocks.text: A ladybug does not grow the way you do. You get taller, but you keep the same body. A ladybug swaps its body four times. It starts as a tiny yellow egg, stuck to the underside of a leaf in a neat little group. The mother picks that leaf on purpose. She looks for a plant covered in aphids, which are soft green insects that suck juice out of stems. She is leaving her babies in a grocery store. In a few days the eggs hatch. What comes out looks nothing like a ladybug. It is long, dark, spiky, and quick, a little dragon the size of a grain of rice. This is the larva. It hunts aphids all day. Over two or three weeks it can eat hundreds of them. It grows so fast that it splits its skin four times and crawls out bigger each time. Then it stops. It glues its back end to a leaf and becomes a pupa. Inside, almost everything is being taken apart and rebuilt. About a week later the shell cracks. A ladybug steps out, pale and soft, with no spots at all. Over the next few hours its cover hardens and its color deepens. Now it has one job left. Find aphids, and lay more eggs.

blocks.prompt: Small, Red, and Completely Rebuilt
blocks.text: Farmers like ladybugs for a simple reason. Ladybugs eat the insects that ruin crops, and they eat an astonishing number of them. What most people never notice is that the polite red beetle on the leaf spent the first month of its life as something far less charming. Ladybugs go through complete metamorphosis, which means the young form and the adult form share almost nothing. The cycle starts with a cluster of yellow eggs, usually stuck to the shady underside of a leaf. The mother does not choose that leaf at random. She hunts for a plant already infested with aphids, tiny sap-drinking insects, so that her larvae hatch surrounded by food. In three to five days the eggs split open. The larva that emerges is dark, elongated, and covered in bristles, and it moves like a hunter, because it is one. Over the next two or three weeks a single larva may eat four hundred aphids. Its stiff outer skin cannot stretch, so it molts four times, shedding the old covering and hardening into a larger one each time. Then the hunting stops. The larva anchors itself to a leaf and becomes a pupa, a motionless orange case. Inside, its body is dismantled and reassembled into a completely different animal. About a week later the case splits and an adult beetle climbs out, pale yellow and soft, with no spots at all. Within a few hours the wing covers harden and the pigment arrives. Those covers, called elytra, are not for flying. They are armor. The real flight wings unfold from underneath them, and they are so much larger that the beetle has to fold them up like a road map to close its shell. One myth is worth killing. The number of spots does not tell you the ladybug's age. It tells you the species.

blocks.prompt: The Insect That Takes Itself Apart
blocks.text: There is a moment in a ladybug's life when it is neither of the two animals it will ever be. Sealed inside a pupal case on the underside of a leaf, it is largely liquid, its old body broken down and its new one not yet finished. Biologists call this holometabolism, or complete metamorphosis, and it is one of the most successful strategies life has ever produced. Roughly two out of every three animal species on Earth are insects that develop this way. The cycle begins with a cluster of yellow eggs, laid deliberately. The female searches out a plant already crawling with aphids before she lays, because her offspring hatch hungry and cannot travel far. Within three to five days the larvae emerge, and they look like nothing you would call a ladybug. They are dark, tapered, bristled, and fast, and they hunt continuously. A single larva may consume four hundred aphids before it is finished growing. Because its cuticle, the stiff outer layer that serves as its skeleton, cannot expand, the larva must shed it. It does this four times. Each stage between molts is called an instar. Then the feeding stops abruptly. The larva cements its rear end to a leaf, hunches over, and pupates. Roughly a week later an adult forces its way out, pale, damp, and unmarked. The wing covers stiffen over the following hours and the pigment develops. That adult is armed in a way the larva was not. Its color is aposematic, which means it advertises rather than hides. Squeeze a ladybug gently and it will push droplets of foul yellow fluid out through its leg joints, a defense called reflex bleeding. The bitter taste and the loud color work as a pair: the warning is only useful because it is honest. Two details are worth correcting. The spot count records species, not age. And the beetle that lands on your arm may not be local at all. The multicolored Asian lady beetle was introduced to North America to control crop pests and has since spread widely, gathering in houses each fall and outcompeting several native species, including the nine-spotted ladybug that became genuinely hard to find. The insect we treat as a symbol of luck turns out to be a working predator, an imported tool, and, in a few cases, a species quietly being pushed aside.

notes: Family Coccinellidae, about 6,000 species worldwide
Holometabolous development: egg, larva, pupa, adult
Imaginal discs carry the adult blueprint through the pupa
Reflex bleeding delivers bitter alkaloids from the leg joints
Harmonia axyridis was introduced as a biological control

blocks.prompt: Four Bodies, One Animal: What the Ladybug Does Inside the Case
blocks.text: The strangest thing about a ladybug is not the red shell or the spots. It is that the beetle and the animal that hatched from the egg are, in almost every structural sense, two different creatures that happen to share a life. Ladybugs are holometabolous, meaning they develop through four separate stages: egg, larva, pupa, and adult. Insects that develop this way now account for the majority of all described animal species on Earth, which suggests the arrangement solves a real problem rather than merely being odd. The problem it solves is competition. A caterpillar does not compete with a butterfly, and a ladybug larva does not compete with the beetle it will become. Splitting a life into a growth phase and a dispersal phase lets one animal exploit two different roles without ever fighting itself for resources. It begins with placement. The female does not scatter eggs. She searches for a plant already colonized by aphids and lays a tight cluster of yellow eggs on the sheltered underside of a leaf, so that her larvae hatch inside a food supply they are too small to go looking for. Within three to five days they emerge: dark, tapered, bristled, and relentless. Over the following weeks a single larva may consume four hundred aphids. Because its cuticle is rigid and cannot expand, growth requires demolition. The larva molts four times, and each interval between molts is an instar. Then the feeding stops. The larva cements its abdomen to a leaf and pupates, and inside that motionless orange case the most extreme part of the process occurs. Much of the larval body is broken down. What survives the demolition includes clusters of cells called imaginal discs, set aside early in development and held in reserve, each carrying the pattern for an adult structure: a leg, an eye, a wing. The pupa is not a resting stage. It is a construction site working from stored plans. About a week later the case splits and an adult emerges, pale, damp, and entirely unspotted. The wing covers stiffen over several hours and the pigment fills in. Those covers, the elytra, are modified forewings; the actual flight wings are folded beneath them and are considerably larger, which is why a ladybug taking off looks briefly like it is unpacking. The adult is also chemically defended. Handle one roughly and it will exude droplets of bitter yellow fluid from its leg joints, a behavior called reflex bleeding. The bright color is aposematic, an advertisement rather than camouflage, and the system depends on truthfulness: a predator only learns to avoid red-and-black if red-and-black reliably tastes terrible. Two corrections. Spot count is a species marker, not a birthday candle. And the ladybug clustering on your window frame in October may be an immigrant. Harmonia axyridis, the multicolored Asian lady beetle, was released repeatedly in North America as a biological control agent. It worked. It also spread far beyond the fields it was meant to patrol, aggregated in people's houses, and preyed on the eggs and larvae of native ladybugs. Coccinella novemnotata, the nine-spotted, was once common enough to be named the state insect of New York and then became so scarce that researchers ran public searches to find any at all. The lesson is not that the introduction was stupid. It is that an animal released into a system does not read the instructions it was released with.
